title: Seven Curtains
logline: A king's chair of carved wood sheathed in thin gold, chosen in 1692 from a warehouse of gifts 'to make up a regalia', was shown to foreign envoys at night, by lamplight, behind curtains raised one at a time; one envoy wrote that it was gilt, one that it was solid gold, one that it seemed plated. It sits in a glass case now, and the film crosses a dark room towards it in seven stops, on its knees, until the lens is close enough to see how thin the gold is.
human_question: When I see something as good or beautiful, how much of that is in the thing, and how much is in the light, the distance and the way I was brought to it?

place.what_kind_of_place: A national museum: a long white nineteenth-century building in the Italian manner, set back behind a lawn in the leafy administrative quarter of the island's largest city, founded by a colonial governor in 1877. Inside, in a ground-floor gallery, one object in a glass case on a red velvet dais: the throne of the last kings of the hill kingdom, a high-backed armchair of carved wood entirely sheathed in chased gold sheet, set with clear crystals and purple stones, with lions for arm-ends, a sun face at the top of the back, two seated female figures beside it, a worn red velvet seat and a matching footstool, with a crown, a sceptre and a sword on stands beside it. The chair was made in the late seventeenth century, stood in the kings' audience hall for about a hundred and twenty years, was taken in 1815, stood for more than a century in a throne room overseas, and has been here since it was handed back in 1934.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: It is among the most spectacular made things on the island and almost nobody sees it properly: by day it is a gold chair behind reflective glass in a busy gallery under flat light. At night, with the gallery dark and one low warm lamp on it, it becomes what its first foreign visitors describe: a gold seat at the far end of a dark room. The film is a single approach across that room, at the height of a kneeling man, in seven stages, from the doorway to the glass; the chair grows from a glow to a wall of hammered metal, stones and lions, and the last stop is a macro centimetres from its surface. Sound off, it is a complete piece: a dark room, a gold thing at the end of it, an approach, and at the end the discovery of what the gold actually is up close.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Only the camera's distance from the chair. The light is fixed for the whole film: one lamp, low and warm, never brought up, dimmed or moved, so that nothing on screen changes except how near the viewer is. The camera travels on a floor-level track at the eye height of someone kneeling, in seven slow dolly moves each of which stops and holds, the number taken from the seven curtains an envoy in 1762 and a physician in 1821 both describe being raised one after another before the throne was disclosed. It never rises to standing height, never goes round the chair, and there is no drone. The film's treatment is its own in the group: night, interior, one fixed artificial light, a stepped forward approach at floor level, and a payoff that is an arrival at a distance rather than a change in the light.
place.when_it_looks_best: After closing, at night, with the gallery's own lights off and the case lights off if the museum allows it, so that the only light on the gold is the crew's single lamp; outside, the building's façade after dark for one establishing frame. Season does not matter. The one condition that cannot be worked around is the glass: the case front has to be either opened under a conservator's supervision or flagged black on the camera side so that the room and the crew do not appear in it.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: The approach film. A white building at night; a dark gallery; a single warm light at the far end of it, on something gold. The camera, low to the floor, moves towards it and stops, moves and stops, seven times. At each stop the chair is larger and more is legible: first a glow, then a shape, then a high back with a sun face and two seated figures, then lions on the arms with their eyes catching the lamp, then stones, then the chased pattern of the metal, sunflowers and leaves. The last stop is a macro: the edge of the gold where one sheet ends, or the pins that hold it, and the thickness of the metal as one bright line. It is complete without a word: a journey across a room to one extraordinary object, and the object turning out, at the end of the journey, to be a skin. No other film in the group is an approach, is lit by the crew, or is shot entirely indoors at night.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The voice uses the chair's own record. A Dutch council minute of October 1692 selects, from gifts lying in a warehouse, what 'may make up a regalia', and the list is almost entirely things for the eye, the ear and the hand: the everyday world the texts call the sense sphere. Then three foreign envoys, thirty-eight years apart, at a court that by custom received ambassadors at night behind curtains raised one by one, describe the same chair: 'handsomely carved and gilt'; 'a throne of solid gold'; 'it seemed to be plated with gold'. Two of the three words are right. The texts give the film its question and its restraint. They define wanting as the attaching that takes a thing to be good, beautiful, sweet; they say every object has a taste, good, bad or middling, and that wanting only ever comes with the good or the middling; they say it arises when such an object meets a mind that is not seeing it, and they describe that not-seeing as a darkness that covers what the object is. The film does not say that anyone who knelt here was in that darkness, because no record can show it and the texts do not claim to. It says only what the lens finds when it gets close: a thin sheet. And it holds the other half of the teaching in view the whole time: of the fifty-four kinds of mind the texts count in the sense sphere, twenty-four are called beautiful. The chair is beautiful. That was never the question.

sequence.on_screen: Night. A locked wide from the lawn: a long white nineteenth-century façade with columns and a portico, the building dark but for one lit doorway. No people, no traffic in frame.
sequence.voice: In October 1692 a Dutch council resolved to go through the gifts lying in its warehouse and select such of them as might make up a regalia for a king in the hills. The list begins: throne, with accessories. Then gilt leather, two screens, three carpets, a clock, lace, cloth worked with gold and silver flowers, and a thousand bells. Almost everything on it is for the eye, the ear or the hand.

sequence.on_screen: Inside. A long dark gallery, seen from its doorway at the height of a kneeling person. At the far end, one warm low light on something gold. The first dolly move begins and stops.
sequence.voice: The texts call this whole world, of things seen, heard, smelled, tasted and touched, the sense sphere, and they count the kinds of mind that live in it. Fifty-four. Twelve they call unwholesome. Eighteen have no root at all. And twenty-four, nearly half, they call beautiful. The list of gifts is not a list of faults.

sequence.on_screen: Second and third stops. The glow resolves into a high-backed chair on a raised red dais: a sun face at the top, two small seated figures, a lion at the end of each arm. Still no detail in the metal; the lamp does not change.
sequence.voice: In 1762 an envoy named John Pybus reached the king's house at half past eleven at night, through streets lit with lamps. Six curtains were drawn up, one after another, then a seventh at a door at the end of the hall. Behind it, he wrote, was the king, seated on a throne, 'a large chair, handsomely carved and gilt'. He was pulled down by the skirts of his coat onto one knee.

sequence.on_screen: Fourth and fifth stops. The lions fill the frame edge to edge: eyes catching the lamp, chased manes, the clear and purple stones in the border of the back. The camera holds each stop long enough for the eye to settle.
sequence.voice: In 1795 Robert Andrews saw the next king 'seated on a throne of solid gold richly studded with precious stones'. In 1800 William Macpherson wrote that it 'seemed to be plated with gold, set with precious stones'. After the kingdom fell, the physician John Davy wrote: plated gold. One chair; nothing in the record says it changed between them. Two of the three words are right.

sequence.on_screen: Sixth stop, at the glass. The chased surface of the back in raking lamplight: sunflowers, leaves, the sun face's rays, every hammered hollow holding a point of light.
sequence.voice: The texts define wanting as the attaching that takes a thing to be good, beautiful, sweet. They say every object has a taste, good, bad or middling, and that wanting only ever comes with the good or the middling, never with the bad. And they say it arises when such an object meets a mind that is not seeing it, a not-seeing they describe as a darkness that covers what the object is.

sequence.on_screen: Held at the sixth stop, lower on the chair: the worn red velvet of the seat, rubbed pale along its front edge, and the brass of the case's lock in soft focus at the bottom of frame.
sequence.voice: The texts list, among the ordinary occasions of wanting, giving wealth to get things held dear, and guarding wealth once it is got. They also say that the same guarding, done with usefulness in front of it, is not unwholesome. The act is the same on both lists. What differs is the aim, and an aim leaves nothing on velvet or on glass.

sequence.on_screen: Still at the sixth stop: one clear stone and one purple one side by side in the border, the lamp in both. Nothing moves.
sequence.voice: This chair was chosen by a council's resolution, taken in 1815, kept for more than a century in a throne room overseas, and handed back in 1934; in the 1980s thieves removed stones from it, and some of what you see replaced them. The texts sort wanting into eight kinds by whether it comes with joy or flatly, whether a justifying view stands in front of it, and whether it rises by itself or is urged. Every handing of this chair is in the record. Not one of those three things is.

sequence.on_screen: The seventh stop, the payoff: a macro a few centimetres from the surface, at the edge of the gold where one sheet ends against the next, or a line of pins if the surface shows one; the sheet's thickness visible as a single bright line. Held, in silence, for as long as the shot will bear.
sequence.voice: In 1908 a scholar allowed to examine it closely wrote: a large arm chair, covered with repoussé gold plate. Gold beaten thin over a frame of carved wood. From the far end of a hall at night, on one knee, the whole of it is gold. From here it is a skin, and a very beautiful one. The texts never said the beauty was the fault.

concept_merge.why_together: C004 carries the film because its question is the one the chair's record already asks: what is it to see a thing as good, beautiful, sweet? The Margaya defines greed as exactly that attaching [C004-M:L13] and says every object has a taste, good, bad or middling, with greed arising only with the good or the middling and never with displeasure [C004-M:L15]; the Pradeepika says it arises when a pleasing or neutral object such as a sight or sound meets a mind clouded by delusion [C004-P:L41], and describes delusion as a darkness that obscures the nature of the object [C004-P:L39], the not-grasping of what the object is [C004-P:L67]. Three envoys at the foot of the same chair wrote gilt, solid gold and plated; the chair is gold sheet over wood. C005 then supplies the rule that keeps the film from turning that into an accusation: the same act, giving wealth to obtain dear things or guarding wealth once got, appears among the greed-rooted occasions [C005-M:L5] and, done with wisdom and usefulness foremost, among the acts that raise no unwholesome mind [C005-M:L9]. C006 supplies the limit: the eight greed-rooted minds are told apart by feeling, view and prompting [C005-P:L27–L42] [C006-M:L3–L17] and ranked by them [C006-M:L19], and the chair's record, which is full of acts, contains none of the three.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the object is the one thing in this story that did not change, and that everything the texts care about lies elsewhere: in the taste each looker met, in the aim of each hand that moved it, and in dials no document records. C004 alone would make this a film about a misdescription; C005 alone a film about a gift's motive; C006 alone a catalogue. Together they let the most beautiful object in the room stay beautiful while showing, at a distance of centimetres, why beauty on its own proves nothing about the mind that meets it, and why a film cannot read that mind off the gold.

concept_links.why: The sense-sphere minds are those that belong to the world of sense objects [C004-P:L25], fifty-four in all, of which twelve are unwholesome, eighteen rootless and twenty-four beautiful [C004-P:L27] [C004-M:L3]. The Margaya defines greed as the attaching that takes things and persons to be good, beautiful, sweet [C004-M:L13] and says every object has one of three tastes, good, bad or middling, and that the greed-rooted mind never comes with displeased feeling [C004-M:L15]; the Pradeepika says greed arises when a pleasing or neutral sight or sound meets a mind deluded by moha [C004-P:L41], calls moha a darkness that obscures the nature of the object and places it under every unwholesome mind [C004-P:L39], and says the not-grasping of the object's true state is moha [C004-P:L67]. The chair's record is the only one found on the island in which the same object is described on the record, by successive foreign visitors to a court that received envoys at night, in three incompatible ways, and in which the object survives to be examined: that is the concept's own question asked by a document, not an analogy. Three does_not_transfer lines bind the film. 'The sense world is a trap': twenty-four of fifty-four are beautiful, so the chair is shown as beautiful and the last line says so. 'Ignorance means lack of education': the not-seeing in the source belongs to the educated too, so the envoys are never presented as naive, and the film does not say any of them was in the darkness the text describes, since no record can show it. 'Desire is bad, so love is bad': nothing in the film treats reverence for the chair, then or now, as greed. The Pradeepika's moral commentary on contemporary society [C004-P:L55–L69] is not used, beyond the one definitional sentence at [C004-P:L67].

The Margaya's list of the everyday occasions of greed-rooted minds includes looking at beautiful things for the pleasure of it, giving wealth to obtain dear things, guarding acquired wealth and preparing dear objects [C005-M:L5]; seven courses of action, taking what is not given among them, are done with greed-rooted minds [C005-M:L3]. It then exempts the same acts when faith, loving-kindness or compassion is placed foremost, and acquiring, guarding and spending wealth when wisdom is placed foremost with regard to usefulness [C005-M:L9]. The chair's history is a sequence of exactly these acts: a gift selected to make up a regalia, a seizure, a century of keeping, a return, a theft of stones, a museum's guarding. Exemption ruling, read from the source line itself: undecidable for every hand that moved the chair. The 1692 minute records a purpose (a regalia for the king) but not whether trade, goodwill or usefulness stood foremost, so it could fall under M:L5 or M:L9; the museum's guarding is the M:L9 case on its face (guarding with usefulness regarded) but the text speaks of a person's aim and a museum is an institution, so the film does not rule. The does_not_transfer line 'Only intentions matter' is honoured: the theft is named as a taking, not dissolved into motive; 'Minimalism or self-denial is virtue' is honoured: the film never suggests the chair should not have been beautiful or valuable. The digest's caution that the exempt acts are called 'not unwholesome' without being called wholesome is kept: the voice says 'not unwholesome' and no more.

The eight greed-rooted minds are distinguished by three conditions, feeling, wrong view and prompting [C005-P:L27–L42]; the Margaya's first example is a theft done with joy, unprompted, behind a justifying view such as 'there is no fault in taking what the rich have in excess' [C006-M:L3], prompting includes urging oneself [C006-M:L5], and it ranks courses of action above ordinary fondness, view-backed above view-free, unprompted above prompted and neutral above joyful [C006-M:L19]. The film uses C006 for one sentence of restraint: the chair's record contains acts, and the three conditions that decide which of the eight any of them was are not in it. The seizure of 1815 is recorded as a layer and not adjudicated, and no justifying view is put in anyone's mouth. does_not_transfer lines bind it: 'Wrong view must not be mapped onto any community's faith', so no belief about the chair, royal or religious, is called a view in the text's sense; 'Calm means good', so the council's measured minute is not offered as evidence of a good aim.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That the texts define wanting not by what is wanted but by how it is taken: as good, beautiful, sweet; that they give every object a taste and say wanting only comes with the pleasant or the middling; and that they place under every harmful moment a not-seeing of what the object is. That three educated men described one chair three ways, and that only up close does the gold become a sheet. And, just as firmly, that the sense world is not a trap: twenty-four of the fifty-four kinds of mind in it are called beautiful, the chair is beautiful, and nothing on screen can show which mind met it on any given night.
what_must_be_real: The chair itself, filmed as it stands in its case, with nothing added to it, polished, re-dressed or moved. The single lamp is the crew's and the film does not pretend otherwise; it is never presented as a reconstruction of the audience hall, and no curtains, costume or kneeling figure are staged. The envoys' words are quoted as printed: Pybus from the 1862 printing of his account, Davy from his 1821 book, both read in the texts; Andrews and Macpherson as quoted in the 2020 newspaper account, which the voice treats as their words but the record marks as not checked against a primary. The final macro shows an actual edge of the gold sheet; if no edge can be seen from outside the case, the film does not fake one and the payoff changes (see drop_if). No visitor, guard or museum officer is filmed identifiably.
position_hint: Near the start of the group, straight after the film about the conditions under which wanting sharpens: before the films about particular acts of taking, owning and spending, this one sets out what the texts mean by wanting at all, a thing taken as good, beautiful, sweet, and why the thing itself cannot settle the question.
risks: Narrating any historical person's mind. Pybus, Andrews, Macpherson and Davy are named only for what they wrote. The voice never says any of them wanted the chair, was dazzled by it, or was deluded about it; 'two of the three words are right' is a statement about words. Pybus's own note that he was tired, hungry and out of humour that night is left out, because putting a man's mood next to the definition of delusion would narrate him.

Adjudicating the conquest. The 1815 seizure is a layer in the chair's history, stated in one clause with its date and without verb of judgement, and never narrated as anyone's grievance or anyone's due. The 1934 return is stated the same way. Nothing in the film enters the live question of other objects' repatriation.

Treating reverence as greed. Crowds came to see the chair when it returned, and it has national and religious meaning for many people. The C004 digest forbids 'desire is bad, so love is bad'; nothing in the film suggests that regard for the chair is wanting, and no visitor is shown.

Turning 'two of the three words are right' into a gotcha. The film does not mock the envoy who wrote 'solid gold'; the does_not_transfer line on education forbids implying the not-seeing belongs to the uneducated, and the voice never says what caused the mistake.

The camera-as-observer method. The approach at kneeling height borrows the envoys' vantage, but the film never turns the charge onto the lens or the viewer; in this group that method is reserved for another film. The kneeling height is a vantage, not an accusation.

Glass. The case front will show the crew, the lamp and the room unless it is opened or flagged; a film of reflections would lose the payoff. This is the main practical risk and is carried into drop_if.

Over-reading the stones. The theft of the 1980s and the replacement of stones rest on one newspaper account; the chair already carried cut crystal when it was described in 1849. The voice says only that some of what is seen replaced stolen stones, and never says which.

A museum is a building, not a landscape. The film has no drone, no weather and one room; its whole claim to be footage-led rests on the object and the approach. If the reviewer judges that insufficient, the record says so itself (see research_note).
drop_if: The Department of National Museums will not allow filming after hours with the gallery lights off, or will not allow either opening the case under supervision or flagging the glass so that reflections can be eliminated.

No edge, seam or pin line of the gold sheet can be resolved from outside the case at macro distance, and the case cannot be opened. In that event the seventh stop would have nothing true to show, and the film should be rebuilt or the slot reopened rather than finishing on a stone or on velvet.
The chair is taken off display, loaned or under conservation during the production window.

connections.note: The group's frost film, on a colonial hill station's valley floor, is about the conditions under which wanting sharpens (weather, a sound body) and pays off on a touch-feeling turning as the sun reaches one blade of grass. This one is about what wanting takes its object to be, and pays off on an object that does not change at all. Both use C004's guard that the pleasant is not proof of anything; the cinema is deliberately opposite: that film is dawn, exterior, natural light and a locked camera, this one night, interior, one crew lamp and a stepped approach.

A room of other people's ordinary belongings at a bus terminal, most of them never collected, filmed in long patient passes along shelves. This is one extraordinary object whose every change of hands is on record. Both are rooms of objects whose owners' aims cannot be read off the objects; the shapes differ (many anonymous things, no history, against one thing with three centuries of documents) and so does the camera (tracking along shelves against a single approach).

Proposed in the blind GRP-02 selection as a country house turned monastery where the same fruit is boiled for a planter's table and then for the monks' upkeep: C004 and C005's 'the why, not the what' on a still life of jars in window light. To keep the two apart this film uses no daylight, no hands and no still life; its object is a single made thing seen by recorded witnesses, not produce.

Proposed in the blind GRP-02 selection as a seafront lawn whose aim was changed from guns to horses to 'the air' while it stayed the same ground: the C005 thesis on open ground, as a day-long time-lapse. Same district and a related argument (one thing, many aims); opposite cinema (open air, a day, a crowd, a cut between empty and full against a dark room, one object and an approach). If both go ahead the district count moves by two.

selection.reason: Rebuilt from scratch on 2026-09-26 on the blind GRP-02 selection's proposal, which was tested and kept with corrections to its dates and to what the throne's time overseas actually was. It is the only place found on the island where one surviving object is described on the record, by successive visitors, in three incompatible ways about what it is made of, which is C004's definition of wanting asked by documents; its weakness is that it is a museum interior, and that is stated rather than hidden.

review.note: This record's body was replaced in full on 2026-09-26 in the blind GRP-02 re-selection. The previous status was already pending, so no confirmation or rejection has been reset, but under standing decision 9 any earlier reading of this record no longer applies. The concepts are unchanged (C004 primary, C005 and C006 supporting). The location, proposed by Claude, is the throne of the last kings of the hill kingdom in its case at the national museum in the capital: a carved wooden armchair sheathed in gold sheet, selected by a Dutch council in 1692 from a warehouse of gifts, described by three envoys as gilt, solid gold and plated, taken in 1815, kept in a throne room overseas and returned in 1934. The film is shot at night with one crew lamp, as a stepped approach at kneeling height in seven stops, and pays off on a macro of the edge of the gold sheet. The title has changed to follow the film. What to judge: first, whether a museum interior with no drone and no landscape meets the footage-led standard (the record argues the object carries it, and says plainly it is the group's most enclosed film); second, whether permission for after-hours filming with the case opened or flagged is obtainable, without which the payoff does not exist. Corrections to the proposal: the throne was not lent abroad for other monarchs' investitures; it stood in the royal throne room overseas, and the dates given for those investitures in the newspaper and encyclopaedia accounts (1861, 1908) disagree with the Garter records (1855, 1909), so the claim is kept out of the voice.

suggested_location.name: The throne of the Kandyan kings, National Museum of Colombo (Colombo National Museum)

also_known_as.name: The Kandyan throne
also_known_as.meaning: the throne of the kings of Kandy

also_known_as.name: Sinhasanaya
also_known_as.meaning: lion seat, the ordinary Sinhala word for a throne
also_known_as.used_by: Sinhala usage (quoted in the 1934 verse recalled in the 2014 account)

suggested_location.region: Colombo District, Western Province: Sir Marcus Fernando Mawatha, Colombo 07 (Cinnamon Gardens), beside Viharamahadevi Park (verified by reverse geocoding the coordinates to Colombo District; no boundary ambiguity)
suggested_location.why_here: It is the one place where a single surviving object carries C004's question on the record. The throne was described by successive foreign visitors, received at night after curtains were raised one by one, in words that disagree about what it is made of, and it survives intact enough to be examined at a distance of centimetres. The museum dates from 1877 and the chair is among the most spectacular made things on the island. A fallback in a different district is the Magul Maduwa, the royal audience hall in Kandy, where the chair stood and where it was shown for a few days on its return in 1934 (one account); it has the architecture of the audiences but not the object, and would take Kandy up by one.

historical_thread.story: In the Dutch Council proceedings of October 1692, as transcribed by the archivist Edmund Reimers in 1929 at the request of the museum's director Joseph Pearson and quoted by Ismeth Raheem in 2020, the council at Colombo under Governor Thomas van Rhee resumed 'the question of sending the gifts lying in the warehouse here for the King of Kandy' and 'resolved to select such of them as may make up a regalia for His Majesty': 'Throne with accessories, all the gilt leather (in the warehouse), 2 Chamber screens, 3 Carpets, 1 Clock, 8 pieces of lace for cravats, 45 pieces of white lace, one piece of old lace, four pieces of Surat cloth, four pieces of Dutch material with gold and silver flowers and stripe, 1000 assorted bells'. The king then was Vimaladharmasuriya II. Pearson could not say who made the chair: Dutch or French prisoners in Kandy, or the Dutch in the low country with Sinhala decoration; he called its style 'undoubtedly Louis XIV' with Eastern ornament. The chair stood in the royal audience hall under six kings until 1815. Foreign envoys were received there at night: John Pybus of the East India Company, in May 1762, reached the palace at half past eleven through streets lit with lamps, saw six curtains drawn up in turn and then a seventh at a door, and found the king 'seated on a throne, which was a large chair, handsomely carved and gilt, raised about three feet from the floor', before he was pulled down by the skirts of his coat to kneel (Account of Mr. Pybus's Mission, printed from the Madras records, 1862). Robert Andrews in 1795 wrote 'a throne of solid gold richly studded with precious stones of various colours'; Captain William Macpherson in 1800 'a large chair placed on a platform three or four steps high, it seemed to be plated with gold set with precious stones'. The Dutch engraver Johann Wolfgang Heydt drew a Dutch audience of 1736: pillars wrapped in cloth and lit candlesticks down the length of the hall. On 15 February 1815 the throne was taken when the palace was sacked on Governor Robert Brownrigg's orders. John Davy, who arrived after the conquest, wrote in 1821 that 'the royal throne was of plated gold, ornamented with precious stones', that 'night was the favourite time for giving audience', and that ambassadors were shown the king behind 'seven curtains' raised one after another. Charles Pridham in 1849 described a wooden frame 'entirely covered with thin gold sheeting (studded with precious stones)', with amethyst eyes in the lions, a golden sun, cut crystal mouldings, a red velvet seat, and a back 'covered with fine wrought silver'. The chair went to the Prince Regent and later to Windsor Castle, where it stood in the Garter Throne Room; Ananda Coomaraswamy examined it there and wrote in Mediaeval Sinhalese Art (1908) of 'a large arm chair, covered with repoussé gold plate set with gems', mostly amethysts and crystal, a few turquoises, which he called the only ones he had seen in Kandyan work, and chasing he found suggestive of European influence. After a State Council resolution moved on 30 November 1933 and passed in February 1934, it was brought back with the crown and other regalia by the Duke of Gloucester in September 1934, and it was mounted on a dais at the independence ceremony of 4 February 1948. It has been displayed at the Colombo Museum since. In the 1980s thieves broke into the museum and removed stones from the throne, including large amethysts; the damage was restored under Roland Silva.
historical_thread.how_it_binds: C004 asks what the sense-sphere mind is, and its definition of wanting is a way of taking an object: as good, beautiful, sweet, with every object carrying a taste of good, bad or middling, and wanting arising only with the good or the middling, when such an object meets a mind that is not seeing it. The Pradeepika's image for that not-seeing is a darkness that covers what the object is. This chair's record is not an analogy for that; it is a documented case of one object taken three ways about what it is. Three envoys, at a court whose custom, as Pybus and Davy describe it, was to receive ambassadors at night behind curtains raised in turn, wrote gilt, solid gold and plated about a chair that is, by every close examination on record, gold sheet over carved wood. The film cannot say, and does not say, that any of the three was in the darkness the text means, because a record of words is not a record of a mind; that restraint is itself C004's warning that not-seeing is not a lack of education. What the record does show is that the same object was the same object throughout, and the gold was never the variable. C005 and C006 then bind the rest of the chair's life: the gift, the seizure, the keeping, the return, the theft and the guarding are exactly the acts the Margaya lists on both sides of its line between greed-rooted and not, and the three conditions that would place any of them among the eight kinds of greed are precisely what no document of the chair records. The first minute is itself a list of the sense sphere: things for the eye, the ear and the hand, selected to make up a regalia.
what_is_certain: The Dutch Council proceedings of October 1692, as transcribed by Edmund Reimers in 1929 and quoted in the Sunday Times (28 June 2020), record a resolution to select from gifts lying in the warehouse 'such of them as may make up a regalia for His Majesty', beginning 'Throne with accessories'.

John Pybus's account of his 1762 mission, printed at Colombo in 1862 from the Madras records and read here in the Internet Archive scan, describes arrival at the palace at half past eleven at night through lamp-lit streets, six curtains drawn up in turn and a seventh at a door, the throne as 'a large chair, handsomely carved and gilt, raised about three feet from the floor', and his being pulled down by the skirts of his coat to kneel.

John Davy, An Account of the Interior of Ceylon (1821), read here in the Internet Archive scan, states that 'the royal throne was of plated gold, ornamented with precious stones', that night was the favourite time for giving audience, and that ambassadors were shown the king behind seven curtains raised one after another.

The throne was taken from the palace in February 1815, went into the British royal collection and stood in the Garter Throne Room at Windsor Castle (Royal Collection photograph record), and was returned to the island in 1934 with the crown and other regalia, brought by the Duke of Gloucester.
Ananda Coomaraswamy examined it at Windsor and described it in 1908 as a large arm chair covered with repoussé gold plate set with gems, mainly amethysts and crystal (quoted in the 2020 account).
The throne is on display in a glass case on a red velvet dais at the Colombo National Museum, with a footstool, a crown, a sceptre and a sword (Commons photographs of 2014 and 2018).
The museum was founded on 1 January 1877 under Governor Sir William Gregory, to designs by the government architect James G. Smither.
Johann Wolfgang Heydt's engraving of a Dutch audience with the king in 1736 shows cloth-wrapped pillars and lit candlesticks down the hall (legend 'f. angezündete Leuchter').
what_is_disputed: The year of the gift: the council minute is dated October 1692 and the 2020 account says the throne arrived in 1692; the caption of a 2018 photograph, apparently following the museum, gives 1693. Both are kept; the voice uses only the minute's date.

That the chair in the museum is the 'Throne with accessories' of the 1692 list. The 2020 account calls the minute 'irrefutable proof'; the minute names a throne but does not describe it, and the identification is an inference by Pearson and Reimers in 1929. It is probable, not proven, and the voice says only what the list says.
Who made it: Pearson offered Dutch or French prisoners in Kandy, or Dutch makers in the low country with Sinhala decoration. No source names a maker.

What it is made of, by eyewitness: gilt (Pybus, 1762), solid gold (Andrews, 1795), 'seemed to be plated with gold' (Macpherson, 1800), plated gold (Davy, 1821), wood entirely covered with thin gold sheeting (Pridham, 1849), repoussé gold plate (Coomaraswamy, 1908). The descriptions are kept apart and not reconciled; the film's claim is only that the close examinations agree on sheet over wood.

The Sunday Times (2020) misquotes Davy, splicing 'The royal throne was of plated gold, ornamented' onto the next sentence about the king's dress and dating the book 1819; the 1821 printed text, read here, has 'ornamented with precious stones'. The 2020 article also gives 'nine successive rooms' separated by curtains; Pybus (six curtains and a seventh at a door) and Davy (seven curtains) agree on seven, and the film uses seven.

The Windsor investitures. The 2020 account says the throne was 'lent to various members of European Royalty for their investiture ceremonies', naming Victor Emanuel of Italy in 1861, Haakon VII in 1906 and Manuel of Portugal in 1908; Wikipedia says it was used for Garter investitures with the same names and dates. Victor Emmanuel II was invested with the Garter at Windsor on 5 December 1855 and Manuel II in November 1909, so two of the three dates do not fit. What role the chair played at any investiture could not be confirmed, and a 2014 memoir gives only 'oral history' that Queen Victoria sat on it. Kept entirely out of the voice.

Who initiated the return: the State Council resolution moved by George E. de Silva on 30 November 1933 and passed in February 1934 (Wikipedia), against a 2014 memoir that credits 'an imaginative British bureaucrat in the Colonial Office'. And where it was handed over: a reception at the King's Pavilion in Kandy (Wikipedia) or an unveiling at the Magul Maduwa (the 2014 memoir, with a photograph caption). Both kept.

The 1980s theft and the stones seen now: the 2020 account says stones including large amethysts were removed and the damage restored, and its photograph caption says the stones are 'now replaced by cheap crystals'; but Pridham in 1849 already describes cut crystal on the chair. Which stones are original is not established.
Where the chair should be kept: the 2014 memoir records a claim in 1934 by Kandyan families that the regalia belonged in the Temple of the Tooth. Historical, noted here, and not entered in the film.

what_to_film: One locked exterior wide of the museum's façade at night from the lawn, with no people in frame.

The gallery dark, from its doorway, at the eye height of a kneeling person (about 70 cm), with one warm lamp placed low and to one side of the case so that it rakes the chased surface and does not reflect into the lens.
Seven dolly moves on a floor-level track from the doorway to the glass, each ending in a held frame of at least twenty seconds; the lamp is fixed for all seven.
At the sixth stop: the lions' heads and eyes, the sun face, the two seated figures, the border of clear and purple stones, the worn front edge of the velvet seat.

The payoff at the seventh stop: a macro (100 mm macro or longer, lens hood against the glass or the case opened) on an edge, seam or pin line of the gold sheet, with the sheet's thickness resolved as a line of light.
Room tone of the empty gallery at night for the whole film; no music.
suggested_location.access: A public museum run by the Department of National Museums, open by day to visitors for a ticket; filming inside needs the Department's written permission, and after-hours filming with gallery and case lights off, a crew lamp and a floor track needs a specific agreement, a conservator or museum officer present, and probably a location fee. Opening the case is the Department's decision and may be refused on security grounds (the case was broken into in the 1980s); flagging the outside of the glass with black cloth and a lens hood against it is the fallback. No drone is used; the exterior frame is from the ground.
suggested_location.best_time: Any season; after closing time on a weekday night agreed with the museum. Allow a whole night for lighting and the seven moves. The exterior frame on the same night.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only, 2026-09-26. Read in primary text: Pybus's 1762 account (1862 printing) for the night arrival, the curtains, the 'handsomely carved and gilt' sentence and the kneeling; Davy (1821) for 'plated gold, ornamented with precious stones', the night audiences and the seven curtains. Reached only through the Sunday Times (Ismeth Raheem, 28 June 2020): the 1692 council minute and its list, Pearson's opinions, Andrews (1795), Macpherson (1800), Pridham (1849), Coomaraswamy (1908) and the 1980s theft; none of these was checked against a primary, and the 2020 article was found to misquote Davy, so its other quotations should be checked before the voice is recorded. The Windsor investiture claim in the 2020 article and in Wikipedia was tested against the Garter dates and fails for two of three names; it is out of the voice. The Oxford/Manchester chapter 'The return of the throne: the repatriation of the Kandyan regalia to Ceylon' (in Crowns and Colonies) exists and was not read. District verified by reverse geocoding (Colombo District, Western Province). District budget: Colombo was at 3 films outside GRP-02/03 and this film takes it to 4; the blind GRP-02 selection also proposes a Colombo seafront film (IDEA-0025), which would take it to 5; GRP-03's selection was not available to check. Commons holds photographs of the throne in its case and of the building, all confirmed by imageinfo query; the fourth image is an engraving of a different place and is captioned so. The strongest objection to this location is the second half of the test: it is a single object in a glass case in one room, with no drone, no weather and no landscape, and it depends on a permission (after hours, lights off, case opened or flagged) that has not been sought. The case for it is that the object is among the most photogenic made things on the island and the documented story asks C004's question more directly than any place found; the reviewer should weigh that against the series' footage-led standard, and the record does not pretend the objection away. Access, permission, the visibility of a sheet edge at macro distance, and whether the case can be opened are all unverified.

unknowns: Whether the Department of National Museums will permit after-hours filming with gallery and case lights off, a crew lamp and a floor track.
Whether the case can be opened, or the glass flagged well enough, for a clean macro.
Whether any edge, seam or pin line of the gold sheet is visible from the front at macro distance.
The primary texts of Andrews (1795), Macpherson (1800), Pridham (1849) and the 1692 council minute, all reached only through a 2020 newspaper article that misquotes Davy.
Which of the stones now on the chair are original.
The chair's actual use overseas, which the sources report with dates that do not fit the Garter records.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location was proposed by Claude and awaits Chathura's review; it has not been confirmed. Quotations from Pybus (1762, printed 1862) and Davy (1821) are documentary and were read in the printed texts; the 1692 minute and the Andrews, Macpherson, Pridham and Coomaraswamy descriptions are documentary but reached only through a 2020 newspaper article; the museum's display and the building are from photographs; everything about access, permission and filming conditions is desk research and unverified. No scene or shot has been filmed.
